Observation Details: Mega*   European Herring Gull (ssp. argentatus)    I first observed this individual on the 13th, and went the same location on the 14th for more pictures to help with identification. After I looked up on eBird, it turns out the bird was first seen by Patrice Domeischel in Feb. 2022 (reported as Larus sp.), then coming back at this location every winter.     Here’s the details of the bird observed from field and pictures I took.  - P10 ‘mirror’ merges completely with white tip.  - Long, pale tongue seen on p10 from underwing.   - Absence of black band on p5 (only a hint of black on left wing but completely absent on right wing)  - Long gray ‘tongues’ on p8-7.  - Darker underwing edge.   - Larger apical spots on primaries.    - Showing obvious streaking on head with blotchy in neck.  - Red on bill restricted to lower mandible.  - Yellow legs and red orbital ring.  - Pale iris.    Based on the features of this gull individual, I confidently identify this bird into an European Herring Gull (ssp. argentatus). Large all-white p10 ‘mirror’ and long p10 ‘tongue’, missing black markings on p5, darker underwing edge and obvious streaking on head with blotchy in neck in winter are typical for ssp. argentatus. Furthermore, darker mantle, yellow legs and red orbital ring are often found in ssp. argentatus from Scandinavia. The rest of the features I listed above are common feature of this species (L. argentatus).   —————————————————————   To rule out other confusion species/hybrids: (primary patterns are always the ‘key’)    Yellow-legged Gull (L. michahellis)  - Missing complete subterminal band on p10-5.  - Missing broad black markings on p5.  - Large apical spots instead of extensive black on primaries (when wings folding).  - Long p10 ’tongue’ instead of extensive black on inner web of p10.  - Red gonys spot restricted in lower mandible instead of ‘bleeds onto upper mandible’.  - Streaked head instead of ‘limited head streaking in winter’.  - Azorean Yellow-legged Gull (ssp. atlantis) has only p10 ‘mirror’.    Caspian Gull (L. cachinnans)  - Missing broad black markings on p5 (CAGU has black on p10-5, sometimes extends to p4)  - Missing ‘long-thin appearance’ bill  - Missing dark iris.     American Herring Gull ‘variant’ (L. smithsonian)  - Medium gray mantle instead of pale gray mantle.  - Missing black markings on p5 (sometimes AHGU have makings on p4 as well).  - Missing ‘bayonets’ appearance.  - Long p10 ‘tongue’ instead of short ‘tongue’.  - Reddish orbital ring instead of orange    Yellow-legged Gull/Lesser Black-backed Gull x Herring Gull   Yellow-legged Gull x Lesser Black-backed Gull  - Any types of these hybrids show subterminal band on p10.  - Some types of Lesser Black-backed Gull x Herring Gull/ Yellow-legged Gull show p10 ‘mirror’ only.  - Any types of these hybrids show black band on p5.  - Some types of Lesser Black-backed Gull x Herring Gull/ Yellow-legged Gull have black on primaries extend to p4.    Species below can be easily rule out:  Yellow-footed Gull & Western Gull  - Both of these species have p10 ‘mirror’ only  - Both of these species have bold white trailing edge    References:   Macaulay Library (pictures for hybrids)  Harrison, Peter, et al. Seabirds: The New Identification Guide. Lynx, 2021.   Muusse, Mars, et al. Gulls of Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East: An Identification Guide. Princeton University Press, Credo Reference, 2024.

Observation Details: Continuing yellow-legged, pale gray-mantled, heavy-billed gull. Very good candidate for European Herring Gull (L. argentatus or L. a. argentatus). Unlike most of American Herring Gulls which often show black markings on p10-p5 and bayonets on p5-8, this individual's black markings on primaries are restricted from p10-p6. Large amount of white seen on p10 and p9 ("mirrors") with larger apical spots on primaries. The similar Yellow-legged Gull should show complete subterminal band on p10-p5 and smaller primary apical spots. I personally not familiar with the hybrids of AHGU and LBBG; but I've been searching and looking at pictures of different individuals on Macaulay Library, which turns out every hybrid individual has black makings reach to p5 at shows much smaller apical spots than this individual seen in the site.

A great irruption year for this species in Eastern Canada, with quite a few currently in the area. When we eventually found this bird, a few photographers were already surrounding it, but he seemed like he was not being bothered, and even faced stared at the ground a few times as if he was hunting. He very curiously rotated his head from one side to the other, watching all of us, and made sure to keep his eye on the songbirds up higher in the tree as well. An incredible owl perched perfectly in the open and looked even more beautiful with the snow landing on him!
